extraction.name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
extraction.description: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) is a large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox. It consists of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages, along with Language Models and baseline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models.
extraction.creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert
extraction.inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Polish
extraction.citeAs: Pratap, V., Xu, Q., Sriram, A., Synnaeve, G., & Collobert, R. (2020). MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research. arXiv preprint arXiv:2012.03411.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Audiobooks were downloaded from LibriVox for 8 languages using data preparation tools from the Libri-Light library. Audio files were downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz and segmented into 10-20 second segments based on silence intervals detected using trained acoustic models. Text sources corresponding to the audiobooks were collected from online domains using domain-specific parsers, pdftotext extraction, manual online searching, or browser copying. Candidate transcripts were generated by matching pseudo-labels generated by acoustic and language models to the source text using TF-IDF and Smith-Waterman alignment.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For non-English languages, some web links for text sources were invalid or redirected to incorrect pages (e.g., spiegel.de), requiring manual searches for alternate sources. Audiobooks were excluded if text sources could not be obtained, if candidate transcripts had a Word Error Rate (WER) > 40% with pseudo-labels, if metadata was corrupted (e.g., missing title, author, or speaker information), or if recordings contained multiple speakers (e.g., dramatic readings).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Audio recordings from LibriVox; textbook sources from Project Gutenberg (gutenberg.org), Internet Archive (archive.org), Christian Classics Ethereal Library (ccel.org), HathiTrust (hathitrust.org), Projekt Gutenberg-DE (projekt-gutenberg.de), and Zeno.org (zeno.org).
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: Numbers in the matched book text were replaced with the corresponding aligned spoken words from the pseudo-labels generated by the acoustic model, resolving issues where numbers could be read in multiple ways or represented unread page numbers.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio was downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz and segmented into 10–20 second chunks based on longest silence frames. Heuristics were applied to handle hyphens and apostrophes based on word frequency thresholds across books. Transcripts were aligned to audio segments using TF-IDF similarity on bigrams and Smith-Waterman alignment.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text normalization was performed using NFKC normalization, removing unwanted characters (punctuations, subscript/superscripts, emojis, escape symbols), removing end-of-line hyphens, and filtering characters outside the language's valid unicode orthography. Audio segments with WER > 40% between pseudo-labels and matched text were filtered out. Multi-speaker audio and books with corrupted metadata were removed, and only the latest versions of duplicate book titles were kept.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Target labels were initially generated automatically by aligning pseudo-labels (from acoustic models and 4-gram LMs) to the source text. For development and test sets, human transcribers listened to the audio while looking at the transcripts and corrected clear and obvious errors (such as diacritics, missing words, and missing apostrophes) to avoid introducing human bias.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Quality of the development and test sets was analyzed by calculating Word Error Rate (WER) between automatically generated transcripts and human-rated transcripts across languages, showing error rates ranging from 1.93% (Spanish dev) to 12.64% (Portuguese dev).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: TDS Convolutions acoustic models trained with ASG loss, wav2letter@anywhere, wav2letter++, KenLM toolkit, Smith-Waterman alignment algorithm, SVM gender classifier with RBF kernel, pdftotext
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker voice audio and speaker gender (inferred using an SVM gender classifier trained on LibriSpeech acoustic features).
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Aims to promote open research in large-scale training of speech recognition systems, multilingual ASR, and Text-To-Speech (TTS) research by providing freely available open-license multilingual data.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Significant language imbalance exists, with English comprising ~44.5K hours and non-English languages totaling ~6K hours (ranging down to ~100 hours for Polish). Development and test sets were explicitly balanced for gender and duration. Human transcribers were instructed to only correct clear and obvious errors to avoid introducing annotator bias.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Number replacement heuristic relies on acoustic model pseudo-labels, which may not always be completely accurate. Language models for low-resource languages such as Polish suffered from high out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rates (13.39%). Domain is restricted to read public-domain audiobooks.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Acoustic modeling and Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) benchmarking, training, validation, and testing; low-resource/limited-supervision ASR benchmarking (standard 10h, 1h, and 10min splits); Language Modeling (LM); Text-to-Speech (TTS) research.
